source.title: What Scales in Cross-Entropy Scaling Law?
source.authors: Junxi Yan; Zixi Wei; Jingtao Zhan; Qing-Yao Ai; Yi-Qun Liu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper fits cross-entropy against model size and argues that its scaling can break down at large sizes because only one component scales robustly. It also compares fit quality across datasets and model families.
record.gate_note: The paper reports cross-entropy and decomposed-component fits across model sizes, and component shares across model sizes. These bear on the claim. It does not report a small-run-to-large-run held-out extrapolation test or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation experiment. Figures and cited studies are not recorded as independent results unless the paper itself reports the outcome.
record.test_reason: The study fits held-out cross-entropy against non-embedding parameters across 32 off-the-shelf pretrained models (14M–70B) on three corpora (Table 1), which bears on V1. Its main argument is that the cross-entropy law needs restating because only one component (Error-Entropy) scales, which makes this T5. The component R², exponent-difference and share results measure a different construct (decomposed terms, not the loss itself) and are recorded under fits_no_version. The paper does not measure a bend in its own cross-entropy curves; the breakdown is cited from other work and explained through component shares.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that only Error-Entropy truly scales, and even fits better than cross-entropy. Self-Alignment and Confidence do not scale. Error-Entropy's declining share explains why CE scaling, accurate at small scale, slows at large scale. They also propose a Confidence-penalised training loss, but they do not evaluate it.
record.recipe_differences: Decomposes cross-entropy into Error-Entropy, Self-Alignment, and Confidence, then fits log-log regressions over pretrained model families and datasets; it is not a replication of the original scaling-law experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Fit quality varies across dataset and model-family conditions. The paper uses non-embedding parameter counts and log-log linear regression; it does not experimentally vary those fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Splitting cross-entropy into Error-Entropy, Self-Alignment and Confidence, only Error-Entropy follows a power law in non-embedding params (R² up to 0.99, mixed-family 0.72–0.90). Self-Alignment and Confidence fit poorly in most mixed-family settings (R² 0.02–0.36). Error-Entropy's exponent is closest to CE's.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The rank-based Error-Entropy component of LM loss follows a power law in model size at least as cleanly as cross-entropy, while the probability-calibration components do not.

fits_no_version.finding: Error-Entropy's share of cross-entropy declines with model size (about 80–90% at small sizes), which the authors offer as an explanation for the cited slowing of CE scaling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The non-scaling share of LM loss grows with model size, predicting deviation of CE from a pure power law.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the scaling-fit statistics. The scale analysis is observational across pretrained models and families rather than a controlled training sweep; cross-entropy fit quality is notably weaker in some mixed or GitHub settings. Several component-share results are presented only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: None; 60 rows retained. The paper also reports training-dynamics plots and a compensated training objective, but those results do not directly test the listed scaling-law versions. The appendix adds Meta-Llama-3.1-405B to qualitative figures without tabulated per-model fit values.

untested.parts: Scaling in training tokens or compute. Controlled sweeps with the other factors non-bottlenecked: the models differ in data, tokenizer and training length.
All of it. No small-to-large extrapolation.
All of it. Text LMs only; GitHub code is still text pretraining evaluation.
No CE exponents are compared across fitting choices, and no allocation results are reported. The CE bend is cited from others, not measured in the paper's own CE fits.

missing.what: Qualitative CE-vs-size plots across 16 models (14M–70B): CE shows clear scaling, but on GitHub some CE points lie far from the fitted line.
An extended plot over the 32 models plus Llama-3.1-405B; the authors say CE still shows clear scaling and conclusions are unchanged.
Which models make up each family's fit, and each family's size range (from Table 5): Pythia 1.2M–6.4B, Qwen 358M–70B, GPT 85M–1.5B. The rows give 'not stated'.

record.verdict_notes: This is an observational study across heterogeneous off-the-shelf models, not controlled training sweeps. The evaluation text may overlap training data, e.g. Pythia on Pile-GitHub and Wikipedia for many models. No uncertainty is given for any fit. The paper does not demonstrate the CE breakdown with its own numbers: its CE fits are mostly good, and the bend is cited from Kaplan, OpenAI and others. This is why V7 is left untested and the component results are under fits_no_version. The record's V7 labels are dropped. The |Δ| formula in the text lacks absolute-value bars, a minor typo. Its text also quotes mixed-model Confidence R² as 0.1002/0.0625/0.2116, but those are the Table 2 |Δ| values; Table 1 gives 0.0202/0.0492/0.0203.

versions.untested_parts: Tests held-out cross-entropy scaling with model size across evaluated models and datasets. Does not independently sweep training tokens or compute while holding the other factors non-bottlenecked.
No prediction of larger-run loss from fits on smaller runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted growth rates for optimal parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The evaluations are on text datasets and pretrained language models; other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
No downstream task performance is evaluated.

Shows variation in fit quality across datasets and model families and argues that cross-entropy can deviate at large model sizes. Does not vary parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, or fitting methods experimentally.
